description: We want to build a useful solution for monitoring astronaut health during long-duration space missions. Our team has skills in web development, programming, data analysis, design, research, and communication. We welcome creative, hardworking people who are interested in space, health, AI/data, software, UI/UX, or content creation and want to learn and build together.
summary:
STAR PLUS is an offline-first health self-check app for astronauts, built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions”. On a Mars transit, a reply from Earth can take up to 44 minutes, so every screen works without a network.

Astronauts track 22 health indicators: vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, oxygen saturation), sleep, mood and stress, food and fluids, radiation dose and cabin air. They can enter readings by typing, through a guided 11-step daily check, from Bluetooth devices, with the camera (reading a device display or fingertip heart rate), by voice, with a reaction test or with a questionnaire. Each reading is checked on the device against published safety limits and the astronaut’s own 30-day baseline. It is then shown as green, amber, red or grey, with the reason, a cited source and “What to do”.

Emergency first aid needs no login. Live NASA DONKI space weather feeds the radiation card. The glucose chart is compared with Inspiration4 crew data from NASA OSDR (OSD-575). When the link to Earth returns, results sync so flight surgeons and Mission Control can review the whole crew. The same offline approach could help people in Antarctica, at sea or in remote clinics. The demo uses synthetic data only. STAR PLUS is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
1. What does STAR PLUS do and how does it work?

STAR PLUS has three roles. Each one signs in with a demo account on the live app.

Astronaut:

  • Today: overall status, the measures to watch, mission readiness and live space weather.
  • Self-check: record any of the 22 indicators through any input method, or follow "Today's check" (11 steps with a progress count, a reminder and streaks).
  • Result: a colour-coded status for each measure (nominal, watch, critical or no baseline yet), the reason, a cited source and "What to do". A critical result links straight to Emergency.
  • Body map: a 3D male or female figure with five clickable body systems. Each one shows what it does, why it matters in space, its status and the latest readings.
  • History: charts over time with the astronaut's personal baseline band. The glucose chart also shades the Inspiration4 crew range from NASA OSDR OSD-575.
  • Hazards: NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, what each one does to the body, the countermeasures and the measures tracked for each.
  • Medicines: an onboard formulary with sources. Doses always follow the flight surgeon or the mission protocol.
  • Progress: points for completing checks (never for the values themselves), ranks, streaks and mission patches.
  • Emergency: first-aid steps that work offline and without a login.

Flight surgeon:

  • A crew board showing every crew member's status.
  • Detail for each crew member.
  • A reports inbox, where reports can be acknowledged.

Mission Control: a crew-wide view of alerts and overall crew health.

How a result is decided:

  • The published safety limit is checked first (NEWS2, ACC/AHA, ADA, AASM, NASA-STD-3001).
  • Then the reading is compared with the astronaut's own 30-day baseline.
  • A small machine-learning model, trained on synthetic data, is shown separately as a grey "Model view". It never changes a status or a next step.

Settings switch the environment (ISS, Mars transit, Moon base, surface rover) and the mission phase (pre-flight, in flight, surface, post-flight). They also simulate the communication delay and blackouts.

The app works offline. A service worker keeps the pages available, and readings are stored on the device in a queue. The queue syncs with the backend when the link returns. "Explain more simply" works offline: its explanations were written in advance from cited text. "Ask about your result" gives a labelled AI answer from cited sources when the device is online.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Astronauts can check and understand their own health without waiting for Earth.
  • Each result explains itself: the reason, the source and the next step, not just a number.
  • Personal baselines catch changes that a fixed limit would miss.
  • Flight surgeons and Mission Control see the whole crew and know whom to look at first.
  • Emergency steps are always one tap away, with no login and no network.
  • Colour is always paired with an icon and a word, so status is clear even without colour.
  • Uses on Earth: Antarctic research stations hold about 5,000 people in summer and 1,100 through the winter (CIA World Factbook). About 2.57 million seafarers crew the world's merchant ships (BIMCO/ICS 2026). They, and remote clinics, face the same wait for a doctor.

3. What is the intended impact?

Safer long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where medical help from Earth is delayed or cut off. STAR PLUS lets the crew act on their own readings with cited guidance, and it gives the medical team a clear picture of the crew as soon as contact returns.

We ran an expert walkthrough of the live demo, fixed what it found and prepared a 15-minute user-test kit (five tasks and the System Usability Scale). Next steps: test with real users, have clinicians review the safety limits and texts, and check the app with real sensors.

4. What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4; Serwist service worker and IndexedDB for offline use; Recharts for charts; three.js for the 3D body; Tesseract.js for reading device displays with the camera. Deployed on Vercel.
  • Backend: Cloudflare Worker with a D1 database and R2 storage; Better Auth for sign-in; rate limits; a nightly reset of the demo accounts.
  • Machine learning: Python, logistic regression trained on a reproducible synthetic dataset (180 invented astronauts, 1,260 records), checked on held-out people.
  • Testing: Vitest unit tests and Playwright browser tests.
  • Tools: Git and GitHub. MIT licence.
  • Hardware: no custom hardware. Any phone or laptop with a browser; the camera; Bluetooth health devices through Web Bluetooth, where the browser supports it.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

  • Every result cites its source. Nothing is an unexplained number.
  • Published safety limits always come first. Personal baselines add early warning, and the AI model only advises: it can never override a limit.
  • It is built for the gap between the crew and Earth: offline by default, with a simulated delay and blackouts, and syncing when contact returns.
  • Points reward doing the check, never the values, so nobody is pushed to report "good" numbers.
  • One system serves three roles, from one astronaut's self-check up to the whole crew's view in Mission Control.
  • Real NASA data is used honestly. Live DONKI space weather and the Inspiration4 crew range give context, and the synthetic demo data is labelled everywhere.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  • Space environment: communication delay, blackouts, radiation, altered gravity and isolation (NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight).
  • Safety: STAR PLUS is not a medical device. No clinician has reviewed the limits yet. Medicine doses are left to the flight surgeon, and emergencies always point to first aid and the crew.
  • Data honesty: real astronaut medical records are protected, so all demo data is synthetic, built from published group-level statistics and labelled in the app. Every reading records whether it is real, synthetic or from a simulated device.
  • Usability and accessibility: one measure per screen in the daily check, plain-language explanations, and colour always paired with an icon and a word.
  • Privacy: each role sees only what it needs.
  • Feasibility: a working web prototype that runs on any device, built within the hackathon.
